400.title: The stars, the moon, the sun, again
400.hook: Ibrahim's search returns in its full setting (6:74–79)
400.howItsDone: Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet opening his prayer with a supplication that includes 6:79, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, and some Muslims open their prayer with it today.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: ghayb, the unseen. Your line was not a leaf unknown. Did you remember the leaf when something small went unnoticed? Today, an old friend comes back. Day four hundred.
screen: `GHAYB — NOT A LEAF UNKNOWN.`

segments.voice: Three hundred sixty-eight days ago, on day thirty-two, you met a young man looking up at a star, then the moon, then the sun, watching each one set. You heard him say, I love not things that set. That was the scene on its own, like a single photo. Today the Qur'an hands you the whole roll of film. Because in surah six, the star is not where the story begins. It begins with an argument between a son and his father, and it ends with a question about who is truly safe.
screen: `DAY THIRTY-TWO, AGAIN.` → `THE WHOLE ROLL OF FILM.` → `A SON, A FATHER, A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Verse seventy-four. Ibrahim says to his father, whom this verse calls Azar: do you take idols as gods? I see you and your people in plain error. Commentators differ on the name Azar: some take it as his father's name, others as a title or another relative, since the Bible calls Abraham's father Terah. Then verse seventy-five: Allah showed Ibrahim the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those who are certain. Only then comes the night sky: the star, the moon, the sun, each one setting. And when the sun goes down, Ibrahim turns. In Pickthall's words: “Lo! I have turned my face toward Him Who created the heavens and the earth,” as one upright by nature, and not one of those who set up partners. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying it in the supplication that opened his prayer, right after the first Allahu akbar. Then his people argue with him, and he asks them a question: which of us has more right to feel safe? Me, who fears no idol, or you, who don't fear associating partners with God? Verse eighty-two answers: those who believe and don't mix their faith with wrongdoing, they have safety. A hadith in Bukhari says that verse frightened the companions: which of us has never done wrong? And the Prophet explained that the wrong here means associating partners with God. Verse eighty-three closes the scene: that was Our argument, which We gave Ibrahim against his people. So the stars were never just stargazing. They were Ibrahim's answer, given in the place everyone could see it: the sky.
screen: `IBRAHIM AND AZAR.` · `SHOWN THE KINGDOM OF THE HEAVENS.` · `I HAVE TURNED MY FACE.` · `WHO HAS MORE RIGHT TO SAFETY?` · then, large: `LOVE WHAT DOESN'T SET.`

segments.voice: If you can, watch the sunset tonight. If not, sit now and picture the last one you remember. Go back to day thirty-two in your mind: the star, the moon, the sun. What were you holding onto then that has since set? A worry, a plan, a person, a phone you loved. Notice it. If you pray, you can say Ibrahim's line: I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth. If not, let your eyes rest on the sky. The bell holds the time.
The stars. Ibrahim's search in its full setting: the argument with Azar, the kingdom of the heavens shown, the turning of the face, and the question of who is safe. Today's word.

401.title: Seed and stone split open
401.hook: Allah splits the grain and the date-stone, brings the living from the dead (6:95)
401.howItsDone: Muslims read 6:95–99 as signs in agriculture and the sky; planting trees is widely encouraged as ongoing charity, following hadith in Bukhari and the Musnad of Ahmad.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stars, Ibrahim's search in its full setting. Your line was love what doesn't set. Did you catch the sunset? Today, from the sky down into the soil. Day four hundred one.
screen: `THE STARS — LOVE WHAT DOESN'T SET.`

segments.voice: Pick up a date pit after you've eaten the fruit. It's hard as a pebble, dry, with a little groove down one side. You could keep it in a drawer for a year and it would look exactly the same. It looks finished. Dead, even. And yet bury it in warm, wet soil, wait, and one day that stone cracks from the inside and a green shoot pushes out. Nobody pried it open. Surah six, verse ninety-five, points straight at that moment and says who did.
screen: `A DATE PIT, HARD AS A PEBBLE.` → `IT LOOKS FINISHED.` → `IT CRACKS FROM THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The verse says Allah is the one who splits the grain and the date-stone. Two Arabic words carry it. Habb: a grain, a seed, the kind you'd scatter for planting. And nawa: the hard pit inside a date, the stone. The verb is falaqa, to split, to cleave open. Its root names the daybreak too. The very next verse calls Allah faliq al-isbah, the one who splits open the dawn, and the second-to-last surah of the Qur'an, al-Falaq, takes its name from the same root. Seed and morning: two things that open from inside, on time, every time. Then the verse goes further: He brings the living out of the dead, and the dead out of the living. Commentators gave many examples. The green plant out of the dry seed, and the dry seed out of the plant again. The chick out of the egg. And, some said, a believer born to people who didn't believe, and the reverse. The verse ends with a question: such is Allah, so how are you turned away? It's an argument made with things you can hold. And the Prophet ﷺ cared about planting. A hadith in Bukhari says that when someone plants a tree and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for the one who planted it. Another report, in the Musnad of Ahmad, says that even if the Hour is coming and you have a palm shoot in your hand, plant it. A seed is a small act of trust. You can't make it split. You only put it where it can.

segments.voice: If you have a seed, a pit, a bean or a grain of rice nearby, hold it in your palm. If not, picture one. Feel how hard it is, how finished it looks. Breathe. 402.title: No vision grasps Him
402.hook: eyes do not comprehend Him, and He comprehends all vision (6:103)
402.howItsDone: Muslims cite 6:103 in teaching that Allah is beyond physical sight, and the hadith of Jibril's definition of ihsan, worship as though you see Him, for He sees you, is often taught alongside it on sincerity in prayer.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: seed and stone split open. Your line was the seed splits. Did something get planted, or watered? Today, a verse about eyes, and what they can't hold. Day four hundred two.
screen: `SEED AND STONE SPLIT OPEN — THE SEED SPLITS.`

segments.voice: Try to see your own eyes. Not in a mirror, that's a reflection. Directly. You can't. The thing you see with is the one thing you can never look at. Now try the other direction: try to take in the whole ocean from a beach. Your eyes give up at the horizon. Human sight is a wonderful tool, and it has edges on both sides. Surah six has just walked through stars, seeds and dawn, all things you can see. And then, verse one-oh-three, it names the one thing sight can't reach.
screen: `TRY TO SEE YOUR OWN EYES.` → `THE OCEAN ENDS AT THE HORIZON.` → `WHAT SIGHT CAN'T REACH.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision. He is the Subtile, the Aware.” The Arabic verb is adraka: to reach, to overtake, to catch up with and take in completely. Eyes don't catch up with Allah. Allah catches up with every eye. And the two names at the end fit. Al-Latif: the subtle, so fine He passes beneath notice, and also the gentle, the kind. Al-Khabir: the one who knows the inside of things. This verse has a long history in Muslim thought. Aishah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ, recited it when she was asked whether he had seen his Lord; her answer, in Bukhari, was no, though other companions, Ibn Abbas among them, are reported to have held a different view. Scholars have also asked about the next life. Sunni theologians of the Ash'ari and Athari schools hold that believers will see Allah in the hereafter, citing a verse in surah seventy-five about faces looking toward their Lord, and a hadith comparing it to seeing the moon. They read today's verse as saying eyes can't encompass Him, not that they can never see. Mu'tazili theologians and Twelver Shia scholars read the verse as ruling out seeing God with eyes at all, and understand those other texts in another way. The schools differ. The second half is not where the argument lies: He takes in every eye. The hadith of Jibril, in which the angel asks the Prophet about faith, describes ihsan as worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, knowing that He sees you.
screen: `ADRAKA — TO REACH AND TAKE IN.` · `AL-LATIF, AL-KHABIR.` · `WILL HE BE SEEN? THE SCHOOLS DIFFER.` · `IHSAN — HE SEES YOU.` · then, large: `VISION COMPREHENDETH HIM NOT.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and close your eyes. Notice what changes when the main way you take in the world switches off. Maybe the room sounds louder. Maybe your body feels heavier. Now, without opening your eyes, rest in the second half of the verse: eyes don't reach Him, and He reaches every eye. The verse doesn't name a camera or a judge on a screen. It names the Subtle, the gentle one, and the Aware, who knows the inside. Breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
No vision grasps Him. Eyes don't take Allah in, but He takes in every eye: the Subtle, the Aware. Today's word.

403.title: Don't insult their gods
403.hook: don't insult what others call on, lest they insult Allah in ignorance (6:108)
403.howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 6:108 to forbid mocking what others hold sacred, and use it as a classic example of sadd adh-dhara'i', blocking the means to harm; some imams quote it in interfaith settings.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: no vision grasps Him. Your line was seen by the unseen. Did you remember it when no one was watching? Today, a verse about the words we use for what other people hold sacred. Day four hundred three.
screen: `NO VISION GRASPS HIM — SEEN BY THE UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: Every comment section on the internet runs on the same engine. Someone mocks a thing another person loves. The other person mocks something back, a little harder. Within a few replies, both sides are saying things about each other's most sacred things that neither would say to a face. Nobody's mind has changed. Everyone is angrier. Surah six was revealed in Mecca, when the Muslims were a small group surrounded by people who worshipped idols, and the arguments were real and daily. You might expect the Qur'an to sharpen their tongues. Verse one-oh-eight does the opposite.
screen: `THE COMMENT SECTION ENGINE.` → `MOCKED, AND MOCKED BACK.` → `MECCA, A SMALL GROUP.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “Revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance.” The verb is sabba: to insult, to curse, to abuse with words. Notice what the verse does not say. It doesn't say the Qur'an has stopped disagreeing with idol worship; this same surah argues against it again and again, with stars and seeds and reasons. What it forbids is the insult. Disagree, explain, argue in the best way, as surah sixteen puts it: with wisdom and good counsel. But don't revile. And the reason is practical: insult what they call on, and they may revile Allah in return, out of ignorance. The verse goes on: to every community We have made their own deeds seem fair to them, and they will return to their Lord, who will tell them what they used to do. In other words, people hold dear what seems fair to them. Mock it, and the mockery comes back aimed at what you hold dear. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim works the same way. The Prophet ﷺ said one of the gravest sins is cursing your own parents. The companions asked, who would curse their own parents? He said: you insult another man's father, and he insults yours. Scholars built a principle from verses and hadith like these, sadd adh-dhara'i': closing the doors that lead to harm. Something permitted in itself can become forbidden when it reliably leads somewhere worse. A rude joke about someone else's faith is one of those doors.

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a faith or a practice that isn't yours, one you've joked about, or heard joked about. Now think of one respectful sentence you could say about their faith, something true, said the way you'd want yours spoken of. Hold that sentence until the bell. The bell holds the time.

404.title: Come, I will tell you
404.hook: a list: no partners, kindness to parents, don't kill children for poverty, fair measure, keep promises (6:151–152)
404.tomorrow: My prayer, my life, my death
404.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often present 6:151–153 as a summary of core duties, and some memorize them as a set; Ibn Mas'ud's remark about the Prophet's sealed testament is often quoted with them.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't insult their gods. Your line was don't insult. Did you speak of someone's faith with respect? Today, an invitation, and a list. Day four hundred four.
screen: `DON'T INSULT THEIR GODS — DON'T INSULT.`

segments.voice: At a family gathering, an elderly relative waves you over. Come here, sit, I want to tell you something. You lean in, expecting a story. Instead they count off on their fingers the few things that actually matter. Be good to your parents. Don't cheat anyone. Keep your word. It's not a lecture. It's what's left after a long life of finding out. Near the end of surah six, after a long argument about food rules and customs the surah rejects, the Prophet ﷺ is told to say one word to the people: come.
screen: `COME HERE, SIT.` → `COUNTED ON THE FINGERS.` → `ONE WORD: COME.`

segments.voice: Verse one-fifty-one, in Pickthall's words: “Say: Come, I will recite unto you that which your Lord hath made a sacred duty for you.” The Arabic word for come is ta'alaw. Lexicons connect it to a root about height, so the call has a sense of come up, rise to this. Then the list. Don't set up anything as a partner with Allah. Be good to your parents. Don't kill your children out of poverty: We provide for you and for them. Don't go near shameful deeds, open or hidden. Don't take a life Allah has made sacred, except by right. Verse one-fifty-two keeps going. Don't touch an orphan's property except to improve it, until they come of age. Give full measure and full weight, in fairness. When you speak, be just, even if it's about a relative. Keep the covenant of Allah. And verse one-fifty-three: this is My straight path, so follow it, and don't follow other paths that scatter you. Some readers count ten items here, and hear an echo of the ten commandments Jews and Christians keep; the Qur'an's list stands in its own words. An early companion, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, is reported in Tirmidhi's collection to have said: whoever wants to read the testament of the Prophet ﷺ, with his seal on it, let them read these verses. And look at what's on it. Almost none of it is about ritual. It's about parents, children, orphans, scales, speech and promises. The sacred duty is mostly how you treat the people right in front of you.
screen: `TA'ALAW — COME UP, RISE TO THIS.` · `PARENTS, CHILDREN, ORPHANS.` · `FULL MEASURE, JUST SPEECH.` · `THE TESTAMENT, SEALED.` · then, large: `COME, I WILL RECITE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and count the list slowly on your fingers: no partners with Allah, parents, children, nothing shameful, life is sacred, orphans, fair measure, just speech, keep promises, the straight path. Don't rush. When you reach the end, go back and stop on the one that catches. Maybe it's a call to a parent. Maybe it's a promise half kept. Choose that one for today. The bell holds the time.

405.title: My prayer, my life, my death
405.hook: say, my prayer, my sacrifice, my life and my death are for Allah (6:162)
405.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite 6:162–163, often together with 6:79, as part of the opening supplication of the prayer after the first takbir; practice varies by school, and some use a shorter opening instead.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: come, the invitation, and the list counted on the fingers. Your line was come, I'll recite it. Which one did you keep? Today, the last great line of surah six. Day four hundred five.
screen: `COME — COME, I'LL RECITE IT.`

segments.voice: People write mission statements for companies, for nonprofits, for their own lives. Plenty of them end up in a drawer. Surah six closes with one that fits in a single breath, and it isn't stuck in a drawer. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying it at the very start of the prayer, right after Allahu akbar and before al-Fatiha, and some Muslims open their prayer with it today. For them, it's the first thing said once the prayer begins.
screen: `A MISSION STATEMENT.` → `ONE BREATH LONG.` → `SAID AT THE START OF THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Verse one-sixty-two, in Pickthall's words: “Say: Lo! my worship and my sacrifice and my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” Four things, in Arabic four short words with the same ending, the i that means my. Salati: my prayer. Nusuki: my sacrifice, my acts of devotion; the word covers the offering at Eid and, for some commentators, every rite of worship. Mahyaya: my living. Mamati: my dying. Notice how the list grows. It starts with prayer, a few minutes a day. Then devotion, a bit wider. Then my whole life: the commute, the dishes, the job, the friendships. Then even the moment of death. Nothing is left over as mine alone. The next verse adds: He has no partner. This I am commanded, and I am the first of those who submit. Ali is the one who reports it, in Muslim's collection: the Prophet's opening joined these verses with the line from five days ago, I have turned my face toward Him. And this is the end of surah six. It closes three verses later by saying Allah made people successors on the earth, raising some above others in rank to test them in what He has given. So al-An'am began with darkness and light, walked through a leaf, the stars, a seed, an eye that can't see Him, a list of duties, and ends here: the whole of a life, handed over in a sentence.
screen: `SALATI, NUSUKI — PRAYER, DEVOTION.` · `MAHYAYA, MAMATI — LIVING, DYING.` · `NOTHING LEFT OVER.` · `SURAH SIX, CLOSED.` · then, large: `FOR ALLAH, LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Walk through your day in four steps, as the verse does. First, any moment of prayer or stillness you'll have. Then, any act of giving. Then the ordinary hours: work, errands, meals, people. Then, gently, the fact that this day is one of a number. If you pray, you can say the verse itself, in Arabic or in English. If not, sum up who the day is for in one plain sentence of your own. The bell holds the time.
My prayer. Salati, in surah six, verse one-sixty-two: my prayer, my devotion, my living and my dying, all for Allah. Today's word.

406.title: The garment of piety
406.hook: children of Adam, We gave you clothing, but the garment of piety is best (7:26)
406.howItsDone: Muslims understand clothing as a gift and modesty as part of faith, though styles of dress vary widely by culture; many recite a short supplication from the hadith when putting on new clothes.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: my prayer, my life, my death, and surah six closed. Your line was all of it for him. A week ends today: the stars, the seed, the unseen eye, no insults, the list, the sentence. Now a new surah. Day four hundred six.
screen: `MY PRAYER — ALL OF IT FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Surah seven is al-A'raf, the Heights, named for a scene later in it: a high wall between the garden and the fire, with people standing on its heights who can see both sides. It's one of the longest Meccan surahs, and it opens by retelling a story you know: Adam, his wife, the garden and the tree. When they eat from the tree, the surah says, their nakedness becomes plain to them, and they start covering themselves with leaves from the garden. The first thing humans ever reached for, in this telling, was something to wear.
screen: `AL-A'RAF — THE HEIGHTS.` → `ADAM, THE GARDEN, THE TREE.` → `LEAVES FOR CLOTHING.`

segments.voice: Right after that story, verse twenty-six turns to all of us: O children of Adam. We have sent down to you clothing, libas, to cover your nakedness, and rish, finery, the word for a bird's feathers. Clothing that protects and clothing that looks good: the verse calls both a gift. Then, in Pickthall's words: “but the raiment of restraint from evil, that is best.” In Arabic, libas at-taqwa: the garment of piety, of mindfulness of God. Commentators gave it several meanings: good character, modesty, faith, a sense of shame before doing wrong. They agreed on the picture. There's an outer garment, and there's an inner one, and the inner one is what really covers you. The word libas shows up elsewhere in a surprising place. In surah two, about marriage, the Qur'an says spouses are a garment for each other: close, warm, covering each other's faults. And in the very next verse here, twenty-seven, comes a warning: don't let Satan tempt you as he drew your parents out of the garden, stripping them of their garments. So clothing in this surah is never just fabric. It's dignity, care, protection. Muslims dress in many ways across the world, from Senegal to Indonesia, and modesty looks different from place to place. The verse doesn't settle a dress code here. It ranks the two garments: the one you can buy is good, and the one you can't buy is best.
screen: `LIBAS AND RISH — COVER AND FINERY.` · `LIBAS AT-TAQWA — THE INNER GARMENT.` · `SPOUSES, A GARMENT FOR EACH OTHER.` · `THE ONE YOU CAN'T BUY.` · then, large: `THAT IS BEST.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice what you're wearing right now. Feel the fabric on your shoulders and your wrists. Someone made it, someone sold it, you chose it. Let that be a small thank-you. Then ask: what am I wearing on the inside today? Patience, or a short fuse? Honesty, or a little performance? Choose one quality to put on, the way you'd choose a shirt, and wear it until evening. The bell holds the time.
Libas. Clothing, a garment: given to cover and to adorn, with the garment of piety named as best of all. Today's word.
screen: `LIBAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the best clothing is inside. Today, dress cleanly and modestly, in your own way, and put on the inner garment too. Day four hundred six.

screen: `DAY 406 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EAT, DRINK, DON'T WASTE.`
